description: We're Team Naaah, students from Tashkent University of Information and Technologies (TUIT), who want to turn NASA Earth data into something you can actually hear and see for The Earth Information Jukebox. We're looking for curious people: coders, data fans, designers, and storytellers. You don't need to know everything, just bring energy and ideas. We split tasks clearly, check in often, and keep it friendly. Join us and let's build something useful!
summary:
We built Earth Jukebox, a web app that lets you hear climate change. It takes real records from NASA, NOAA, and NSIDC (global temperature, CO₂, Arctic sea ice, and sea level) and plays each year as a musical note, while a globe and a chart show the same numbers moving. You can play one record on its own, or all four together as a single piece.

Most climate data lives in charts, and plenty of people never look at them or find them hard to read. A rising or falling melody is easier to feel, and it opens the data up to people who can't read charts easily. The app works in eight languages. An AI assistant on the Claude-hosted version can answer questions and control playback. And anyone can load their own CSV and hear it the same way.

We think this matters because people can't act on something they don't understand. Making the data something you can listen to, explore, and share is one small way to close that gap. Right now, the built-in ice and sea level data stop at 2019, but newer official files can be loaded in.
details:
We wanted to find out what climate change sounds like. So we built Earth Jukebox, a little web app where you press play and hear the planet's story, one year at a time.

It takes real records from NASA, NOAA and NSIDC (how much hotter the world has got, how much CO₂ is in the air, how much Arctic ice is left in September, how high the sea has risen) and turns every year into a musical note. As the melody climbs or falls, a spinning globe and a simple chart show the same change, so you can hear it and see it together. You can listen to one record on its own, or let all four play as a single piece.

The idea came from a simple frustration. Climate data usually comes as charts, and plenty of people never look at them or can't read them easily. A melody is something anyone can follow. We wanted people who don't think of themselves as "data people" to feel the trend, and to feel it without having to be told what to think.

We tried to make it welcoming. It speaks eight languages, has light and dark themes, and can read out what's happening on screen. If you have your own numbers, you can paste them in or upload a CSV and hear those too. On the Claude-hosted version there's also an AI helper you can ask questions, like "how much has the temperature risen?", and it can jump to a year or press play for you.

It's built with plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, and we used Claude along the way to help write and test it. We're also upfront about what's missing: the built-in sea ice and sea level data stop at 2019, and the app says so and lets you load newer official files.

If it makes one person stop and listen to a trend they used to scroll past, we'll be happy.
dataRefs: NASA GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (GISTEMP v4)
NSIDC Sea Ice Index (Arctic September extent)
